title: Not my judgment
hook: the tyrant has power over the body, never the judgment (Discourses 1.19)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was lychnos, the stolen lamp. Your line was a clay lamp: replace it simply, and keep what can't be stolen.

Epictetus' old master, Epaphroditus, once sold a slave who made shoes, because he thought the man was useless. Then someone in the emperor's household bought the shoemaker, and he became the emperor's own shoemaker. Suddenly Epaphroditus couldn't do enough for him. How is our dear Felicio, he'd ask. Come looking for Epaphroditus, and you'd be told he was in a meeting with Felicio. Epictetus tells it with a straight face, and lets it sit.
screen: `THE USELESS SHOEMAKER.` → `NOW HE WORKS FOR THE EMPEROR.` → `IN A MEETING WITH FELICIO.`

segments.voice: This is Discourses book one, chapter nineteen: how we should behave toward tyrants. Felicio is the joke that opens the door. Why did Epaphroditus suddenly fawn over his old shoemaker? Not because Felicio changed, but because Felicio was now near the emperor. Then the real question. What frightens people? The tyrant and his guards? No. Nothing that is free by nature can be troubled by anything but itself. What troubles us is our own judgments. So when the tyrant says, I'll chain your leg, the person who prizes the leg begs for mercy. The person who prizes their own will says: if it seems better to you, chain it. Take the body, if you have power over it. But no one, Epictetus says, has power over another person's will. They can threaten, and make choosing costly, but the choosing stays with you. Tyrants come in small sizes, too: a boss who controls your schedule, a relative who controls the family's approval, an online crowd that controls how you feel about yourself. The question works on all of them: what exactly can they touch? Your paycheck, maybe. Your mood, only if you hand it over. Your judgment, never. That's not a promise that standing firm will be painless. It's a map of where the fight actually is.
screen: `WHY FAWN OVER FELICIO?` · `OUR OWN JUDGMENTS FRIGHTEN US.` · `THE TYRANT CAN'T REACH THE WILL.` · `TYRANTS IN SMALL SIZES.` · then, large: `NOT MY JUDGMENT.`

segments.voice: Name one fear that's been pressing on you lately: losing a job, someone's disapproval, a diagnosis, money. Sort it, first what it could touch, my income, my plans, my comfort, my body, then what it can't: what I value, how I treat people, whether I stay honest. Rest your attention on that second list.
Dogma. Greek for judgment, a settled opinion: Epictetus' word for the views that shape our reactions, which no tyrant can touch.
Your line: the choosing stays with you. They can make it costly; they can't make it for you. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some Stoic readers sort a fear into what it could touch and what it can't, keeping their attention on their own judgment and choices.
